topic: Day 2 · Prevention, Rebleeding & Systems — Closing the Loop
speakerAffiliation: Virtual Teaching Hospital · Digestive Diseases & Clinical Governance
speakerBio: Gastroenterologist and clinical-governance lead who built the hospital's GI-bleed care bundle and believes the discharge summary is where most bleeding deaths are actually decided.
lectureHTML:
🎯 The case on the table

It is the readmission that should never have happened. A 63-year-old man was discharged six weeks ago after endoscopic haemostasis of a bleeding duodenal ulcer. He is back tonight with melaena and a haemoglobin of 58. His discharge summary is a masterpiece of the acute — clip, adrenaline, PPI infusion — and a desert of the chronic: his H. pylori was positive and never treated, nobody stopped his ibuprofen, and no one confirmed eradication. The bleed was stopped; the disease was not. This final session is about closing that loop — turning a survived bleed into a prevented one — and pulling the whole sixteen-session conference together.

1 · 🦠 H. pylori — the commonest preventable recurrent ulcer bleed

If you remember one thing from this session: an untreated H. pylori infection is the single most preventable cause of recurrent peptic-ulcer bleeding. Eradication reduces ulcer rebleeding from double figures to low single digits — it is the highest-yield secondary-prevention intervention in the whole field.

💡 Test-and-treat — and confirm cure

Every patient with a peptic-ulcer bleed must be tested for H. pylori, treated if positive, AND have eradication confirmed. Two traps: (1) acute bleeding and PPI use cause false-negative tests — a negative biopsy urease/histology during an acute bleed does not exclude infection, so a negative test in the acute setting must be repeated after recovery. (2) Testing is not treating and treating is not curing — confirm eradication with a urea breath test or stool antigen at least 4 weeks after antibiotics and ≥2 weeks off PPI. Skipping the confirmation step is how resistant infection silently persists and re-bleeds.

Regimen (Maastricht VI): in areas of high clarithromycin resistance or unknown local resistance, use bismuth quadruple therapy (PPI + bismuth + tetracycline + metronidazole) for 14 days as first-line; reserve clarithromycin triple therapy for known low-resistance settings. Tailor to local resistance and prior macrolide exposure.

2 · 💊 NSAID / antiplatelet gastroprotection

The second great preventable ulcer bleed is drug-induced. The rule is simple: if a patient must stay on an NSAID or antiplatelet and has any ulcer-bleed risk, co-prescribe a PPI.

  • Stop the NSAID if at all possible — this is the single best action. If not, use the lowest dose, and add a PPI.
  • Aspirin/antiplatelet for cardiovascular secondary prevention: do not stop it (session 14) — protect with a PPI instead.
  • High-risk combinations (dual antiplatelet therapy, antiplatelet + anticoagulant, prior ulcer bleed, age >65, concomitant steroids/SSRIs): PPI co-prescription is mandatory.
  • Consider a COX-2 selective agent + PPI for the highest-risk patients who genuinely need an NSAID — but weigh cardiovascular risk.

3 · 🩸 Secondary prophylaxis of varices — the combination rule

After a variceal bleed, the risk of rebleeding without prophylaxis is around 60% within a year, with high mortality. Baveno VII is unambiguous: secondary prophylaxis is combination therapy.

🎯 The combination — NSBB + EBL

Non-selective beta-blocker (propranolol/nadolol, or preferably carvedilol) PLUS endoscopic band ligation. The drug lowers portal pressure (the systemic driver); the banding obliterates the local varices. Neither alone is as good as both together — this combination is the standard of care for preventing variceal rebleeding.

  • Carvedilol is now the preferred NSBB in Baveno VII — its additional anti-α1 activity lowers portal pressure more effectively than traditional beta-blockers.
  • HVPG response: the hepatic venous pressure gradient is the gold-standard measure of portal pressure. A "haemodynamic responder" drops HVPG to <12 mmHg or by ≥10–20% from baseline — responders have markedly lower rebleeding. Below the <12 mmHg threshold, varices essentially do not bleed.
  • Band ligation is repeated at intervals until varices are eradicated, then surveilled.
  • TIPS is the rescue for those who rebleed despite combination therapy (and "pre-emptive early TIPS" within 72 h for high-risk acute bleeders — Child–Pugh C or B with active bleeding).

4 · 🔁 Managing rebleeding — the escalation ladder

Rebleeding after initial endoscopic haemostasis is the moment plans must be pre-made, not improvised.

StepNon-variceal (peptic ulcer)Variceal
1st rebleedRepeat endoscopy once — a second endoscopic attempt is appropriate and often succeedsRepeat endoscopic band ligation; ensure vasoactive drug + antibiotics running
If it failsTranscatheter arterial embolisation (angio) — preferred over surgery where availableTIPS (transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt) — the rescue of choice
Last resortSurgery (oversew/resect)Balloon tamponade / oesophageal stent as a bridge to TIPS; surgery/shunt rarely
Endoscopy gets one more chance. After a second failure, stop re-scoping and escalate — angio/embolisation for the ulcer, TIPS for the varix. Repeating a failed endoscopy a third time is how patients die during the delay.

5 · 🛡️ Primary prophylaxis of varices

Prevention before the first bleed. For patients with medium/large varices or varices with high-risk stigmata, offer either a non-selective beta-blocker (carvedilol preferred) or endoscopic band ligation — for primary prophylaxis these are alternatives, not a combination (unlike secondary prophylaxis). Under Baveno VII, patients with clinically significant portal hypertension should be on an NSBB (carvedilol) to prevent decompensation, and small varices with red signs or Child C also warrant NSBB. Screen for varices at diagnosis of cirrhosis; the Baveno "rule of favourable Baveno VI/VII" (LSM <20 kPa and platelets >150) can spare low-risk patients endoscopy.

6 · 🔬 Stress-ulcer prophylaxis stewardship

Carried from session 15 into the prevention frame: stress-ulcer prophylaxis is a stewardship problem. Give it to the genuinely high-risk (ventilated ≥48 h, coagulopathic), prefer a PPI, and — the systems failure we see everywhere — stop it when the risk factor resolves and never let it be continued on discharge. A huge fraction of community PPI use begins as unreviewed ICU/ward prophylaxis. Deprescribing acid suppression that is no longer indicated is itself a bleeding-and-infection prevention measure.

7 · 📊 GI-bleed care bundles & quality metrics

Good outcomes come from systems, not heroics. A modern GI-bleed service is built on bundles and measured:

DomainBundle elementQuality metric
Risk stratificationGlasgow–Blatchford at presentation (score 0–1 → consider discharge)% with documented GBS; safe early-discharge rate
ResuscitationRestrictive transfusion (Hb ~70 g/L)% transfused within restrictive threshold
Timing of endoscopyWithin 24 h of presentation (after resuscitation); urgent for unstable% scoped <24 h; door-to-endoscopy time
Variceal bundleVasoactive drug + antibiotics before endoscopy in suspected variceal bleed% receiving terlipressin + antibiotics pre-scope
Peptic-ulcer therapyDual endoscopic haemostasis + high-dose PPI% high-risk ulcers receiving combination therapy
Secondary preventionH. pylori test/treat/confirm; PPI; anticoagulant restart plan; NSBB+EBL% with documented eradication; % with restart plan
Outcomes—Rebleeding rate, 30-day mortality, readmission, transfusion per case
💡 The 24-hour window (not sooner)

Endoscopy within 24 hours of adequate resuscitation is the quality standard for most upper-GI bleeds. Note the nuance from recent evidence: very early (<6 h) endoscopy in high-risk patients does not improve mortality and may worsen outcomes if it pre-empts resuscitation — resuscitate first, scope within 24 h.

8 · 🧩 Synthesis — the whole conference in one frame

Sixteen sessions reduce to a handful of load-bearing principles that recur across every scenario:

  1. Resuscitate before you localise. ABC, two large cannulae, and a restrictive transfusion target (~70 g/L) — over-transfusion raises portal pressure and worsens outcomes.
  2. Risk-stratify with the Glasgow–Blatchford score — it safely identifies who can go home and who is dangerous.
  3. Suspected variceal bleed = drugs + antibiotics before the scope (terlipressin/octreotide + prophylactic antibiotics), then band ligation; the antibiotic reduces mortality.
  4. Peptic-ulcer bleed = dual endoscopic haemostasis + high-dose PPI, scoped within 24 h of resuscitation.
  5. "Normal scopes" is not "no source" — the small bowel holds the answer (capsule → device-assisted enteroscopy), and age triages the cause.
  6. Special populations break the rules: the cirrhotic INR lies; Heyde's is cured by the valve; uraemia needs desmopressin; mechanical valves need early re-anticoagulation.
  7. The thrombotic clock outkills the bleeding clock — restart anticoagulation after haemostasis, don't stop secondary-prevention aspirin, and always write a restart plan.
  8. Close the loop: H. pylori test-treat-confirm, PPI gastroprotection, NSBB+EBL for varices, and stress-ulcer stewardship. The survived bleed must become the prevented bleed.
☠️ M&M — the loop nobody closed

Return to our opening patient. Six weeks ago his bleeding duodenal ulcer was expertly controlled: dual endoscopic therapy, 72 hours of high-dose PPI, a textbook acute admission. But his admission H. pylori histology — taken during active bleeding and on a PPI — came back negative, and nobody questioned it or repeated it after recovery. His long-standing ibuprofen for knee pain was never stopped. No eradication was given, so none was confirmed. Tonight he is back, shocked, from the same ulcer. Lessons: acute-phase and on-PPI H. pylori tests are falsely negative and must be repeated after recovery; the NSAID is a preventable driver that has to be stopped or PPI-covered; and treating without confirming eradication is not prevention. Every element of his rebleed was foreseeable and preventable at discharge. The acute care was flawless — and the patient still nearly died, because the loop was never closed. That gap, repeated across a whole service, is exactly what care bundles and quality metrics exist to catch.

9 · 🎯 Take-home messages

  1. H. pylori is the commonest preventable recurrent ulcer bleed — test, treat, and confirm eradication (repeat the acute test — it is falsely negative on PPI/during bleeding).
  2. NSAID/antiplatelet gastroprotection: stop the NSAID if you can, PPI-cover if you can't, and never stop secondary-prevention aspirin.
  3. Secondary variceal prophylaxis is a combination: NSBB (carvedilol preferred) plus band ligation; HVPG <12 mmHg or ≥10–20% fall marks the responder.
  4. Rebleeding: repeat endoscopy once, then escalate — angio/embolisation for ulcers, TIPS for varices; don't re-scope a failed lesion a third time.
  5. Primary variceal prophylaxis is NSBB or band ligation (an either/or, unlike secondary), plus NSBB for clinically significant portal hypertension.
  6. Stress-ulcer prophylaxis is stewardship — narrow indications, prefer PPI, and stop it (don't discharge on it).
  7. Build the system: GBS risk score, restrictive transfusion, scope within 24 h, variceal drug+antibiotic bundle, and a secondary-prevention checklist — measured by rebleed rate and 30-day mortality.
  8. The whole conference in one line: resuscitate, risk-stratify, treat the right lesion the right way within 24 h — then close the loop so the bleed never comes back.

moderatorQs.q: A patient with a bleeding peptic ulcer has a negative H. pylori biopsy taken during the acute bleed. Are you reassured?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: No — a negative H. pylori test in the acute setting is unreliable. Both active bleeding and PPI therapy suppress the organism and cause false-negative biopsy urease tests and histology, so a negative result during an acute ulcer bleed does not exclude infection. I would repeat the test after recovery — ideally a urea breath test or stool antigen once the patient is off PPI for at least two weeks. And testing is not the endpoint: if positive I treat (bismuth quadruple therapy for 14 days in high/unknown-resistance areas per Maastricht VI) and then confirm eradication at least 4 weeks after antibiotics and 2 weeks off PPI. Untreated H. pylori is the commonest preventable cause of recurrent ulcer bleeding, so a falsely reassuring acute test is a genuine hazard.

moderatorQs.q: What is the standard secondary prophylaxis after a variceal bleed, and what does Baveno VII say makes it optimal?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: Secondary prophylaxis after a variceal bleed is combination therapy — a non-selective beta-blocker plus endoscopic band ligation, and Baveno VII is explicit that the combination beats either component alone. The drug lowers portal pressure (the systemic driver) while banding obliterates the varices locally; without prophylaxis rebleeding runs around 60% at one year. Baveno VII now prefers carvedilol as the NSBB because its anti-α1 activity lowers portal pressure more than traditional beta-blockers. The physiological target is a haemodynamic response — dropping the hepatic venous pressure gradient to <12 mmHg or by ≥10–20% from baseline, below which varices essentially do not bleed. Band ligation is repeated until varices are eradicated, and TIPS is the rescue for those who rebleed despite combination therapy.

moderatorQs.q: A patient rebleeds from an ulcer after successful initial endoscopic haemostasis. How many times do you re-scope before escalating?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: Once. A single repeat endoscopy after a first rebleed is appropriate and frequently achieves durable haemostasis, so it is worth a second endoscopic attempt. But if that second attempt fails, I stop re-scoping and escalate: for a bleeding peptic ulcer the next step is transcatheter arterial embolisation (angiography), which is preferred over surgery where available, with surgery (oversew or resect) as the last resort. Repeatedly re-scoping a lesion that has already failed twice wastes the critical window while the patient exsanguinates. For variceal rebleeding the equivalent escalation is repeat band ligation once, then TIPS. The principle is: endoscopy gets one more chance, then move up the ladder decisively.

audienceQs.q: When exactly should I confirm H. pylori eradication, and with what test?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Confirm with a urea breath test or stool antigen test — not serology, which stays positive after cure. Timing is the bit people get wrong: test at least 4 weeks after finishing the antibiotics and after the patient has been off any PPI for at least 2 weeks (an H2-blocker or antacid can be used in the interim if symptoms need cover). Testing too early or on a PPI gives a false-negative and misses persistent, often resistant, infection. Confirming cure matters because eradication is the single highest-yield step to prevent recurrent ulcer bleeding — and 'treated' is not the same as 'cured' until you have documented it.

audienceQs.q: How soon after presentation should an upper-GI bleed be scoped — is sooner always better?
audienceQs.answerHTML: The standard is endoscopy within 24 hours of presentation, after adequate resuscitation — not sooner for its own sake. Recent evidence (including a randomised trial in high-risk patients) showed that very early endoscopy at <6 hours did not improve mortality and can worsen outcomes if it pre-empts proper resuscitation and optimisation. So the rule is resuscitate first, scope within 24 h. The exceptions that warrant more urgent endoscopy are the haemodynamically unstable patient who cannot be stabilised and suspected variceal bleeding — and in suspected variceal bleeds you should already have started a vasoactive drug and prophylactic antibiotics before the scope.

audienceQs.q: What are the highest-value metrics to audit for a GI-bleed service?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Anchor on the points where outcomes are actually won or lost. Process metrics: % with a documented Glasgow–Blatchford score (and safe early-discharge rate for GBS 0–1), % managed within a restrictive transfusion threshold (~70 g/L), door-to-endoscopy within 24 h, % of suspected variceal bleeds getting vasoactive drug + antibiotics before endoscopy, and % of high-risk ulcers getting dual endoscopic therapy + high-dose PPI. Then the secondary-prevention loop: % with H. pylori tested/treated/eradication-confirmed and % discharged with a documented anticoagulant-restart plan. Outcome metrics to close the audit: rebleeding rate, 30-day mortality, readmission, and transfusion per case. Those few numbers will expose almost every systemic failure in a bleeding service.
